screens.title: Secure Software Development Life Cycle (SSDLC) Principles
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by framing why security must be part of every step of delivery, not an afterthought. The Secure Software Development Life Cycle or SSDLC extends the traditional SDLC by weaving security activities into requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. That shift prevents costly rework, reduces exploit windows, and creates measurable controls. For example, defining security requirements with functional requirements means authentication, data classification, and storage protections are considered before design decisions lock them out. A well‑run SSDLC applies threat modeling during design to uncover issues like S Q L injection or cross‑site scripting before code is written. It uses secure coding practices and code reviews during development, automated and manual testing during test cycles, and environment hardening for deployment. Finally, maintenance keeps the system resilient through monitoring and timely patches. A common mistake is treating SSDLC as a checkbox project; instead, treat it as continuous engineering. As you study this chapter, think about one system you know and how a single security requirement could have avoided a later incident.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › SSDLC Principles
Secure Software Development Life Cycle
Principles for integrating security across requirements, design, development, testing, deployment and maintenance.
This chapter teaches how shifting security earlier lowers cost, how to apply threat modeling, how to write security requirements, and how testing and maintenance keep systems resilient. You will see practical examples such as specifying password and data handling rules at requirements and using STRIDE during design.
In this lesson
  • Why SSDLC matters and the economics of fixing issues early.
  • How "shift left" changes engineering practices.
  • Threat modeling methods and example mitigations.
Explore Key Topics
Shift Left
Move security into requirements and design to reduce remediation cost.
Threat Modeling
Identify threats, entry points, and mitigations using STRIDE or DREAD.
Testing & Maintenance
SAST, DAST, IAST and ongoing monitoring keep risk controlled post‑deployment.
Visual summary
Requirements
Security requirements, compliance, data sensitivity
Design
Threat modeling, secure design principles
Development
Secure coding, code reviews, dependency hygiene
Testing & Maintenance
SAST, DAST, pen testing and continuous patching
Coming up
We will explore the shift left paradigm, write security requirements, perform threat modeling with STRIDE, and review secure coding and testing practices through practical examples.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the foundational principles and phases of an integrated Secure Software Development Life Cycle, describe the shift left security paradigm and its practical benefits, and identify where security activities belong in each SDLC phase. You will also be able to perform a basic threat modeling exercise using STRIDE to pinpoint likely weaknesses in a design and formulate clear security requirements to include in project planning. These outcomes matter because they turn security from a gate at the end of delivery into engineering choices that save time and prevent breaches. For example, defining credential handling rules in requirements reduces the chance that a later design will rely on weak storage or naive authentication. Over the next screens you will practice mapping threats to mitigations and writing one or two security requirements for a sample feature. That practical work will make the SSDLC concrete and repeatable in your team.

screens.title: What is the SSDLC?
screens.narratorSegment: The Secure Software Development Life Cycle is an extension of the traditional SDLC that embeds security activities and thinking into every phase of delivery. Define the SSDLC as the union of development stages plus explicit security tasks for requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Practically, that starts by making security requirements part of the project scope: classify sensitive data, require strong credential handling, and capture compliance needs. During design, do threat modeling to find attack routes and document mitigations. During development, require secure libraries, coding standards, and code reviews. During testing, run static and dynamic tools and validate mitigations with penetration tests. For deployment, harden runtime and configuration. For maintenance, monitor, patch, and manage vulnerabilities. A concrete example: a login feature should have a security requirement to store passwords with industry‑standard hashing and to rate limit failed attempts. A common misconception is that SSDLC is an add‑on phase at the end of the project; instead, it is a continuous set of activities that move left. Key takeaway: when security is planned, it becomes an engineering decision rather than a last‑minute rescue. How would you capture one security requirement for a simple feature you maintain?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: SSDLC = SDLC + embedded security tasks across all phases so controls are deliberate, early, and measurable.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › What is the SSDLC?
SSDLC — Definition & Phases
An SDLC that integrates security activities at each phase so risks are identified and mitigated early.
Requirements
Define security and compliance needs, data sensitivity, and abuse cases.
Design
Threat modeling and secure design patterns such as least privilege.
Development
Secure coding practices, dependency hygiene, and code review.
Testing & Maintenance
SAST/DAST/IAST, penetration testing, monitoring, and patching.
Explanation & Example
  • Definition: SSDLC means planning and implementing security tasks through requirements to maintenance so controls are deliberate.
  • Why it matters: Fixing a vulnerability in production costs far more than addressing it during design or coding.
  • Concrete example: For login, require hashed credentials, rate limiting, and session controls as part of requirements.
  • Misconception: SSDLC is not just an extra validation step at the end — it is an ongoing engineering practice.
Key Takeaway

Plan security early. Convert controls into requirements and verify them through design and testing.

Common Mistake

Treating SSDLC as a one-time project results in gaps and a false sense of security.

screens.title: The 'Shift Left' Paradigm
screens.narratorSegment: Shift left is a change in mindset: insert security activities earlier in development so defects are found when they cost less to fix. The principle arises from the observation that the cost and effort to remediate vulnerabilities increase sharply the later they are discovered. When a design flaw is corrected at the requirements phase, it may require a single decision; when the same flaw is fixed in production, it may require code changes, retesting, redeployment, and potential incident response. To adopt shift left you change workflows: require security requirements during planning, run threat models during design, and enforce static analysis and code reviews during development. A practical example: adding a requirement to salt and hash passwords removes the need for later emergency rework to replace insecure storage. Common misconceptions include thinking shift left eliminates the need for testing; it does not. Rather, it changes the types of testing earlier and reduces the number of critical issues found late. Key exercises include capturing one security requirement per feature and requiring a short design review that includes a threat model. How would you redesign a planning checklist to ensure a security requirement cannot be skipped?

keyIdea.title: Shift Left
keyIdea.text: Move discovery of security issues earlier—requirements and design—so fixes are cheaper and more reliable.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Shift Left
Shift Left — Process view
Move security tasks earlier to reduce remediation cost and improve design choices.
Requirements: capture security controls and compliance obligations early.
Design: run threat modeling and apply secure design principles to reduce attack surface.
Development: use static analysis, secure libraries, and code review to catch mistakes early.
Concrete Example
If a login feature requires hashed credentials at requirements, design and code will conform; otherwise a late change may touch many modules and disrupt schedules.
Misconception Check
Shift left does not remove testing. It reduces late critical defects and changes the balance of preventive vs corrective work.
Key Takeaway

Adopt a checklist that enforces at least one security requirement and a short design review before development starts.

screens.title: Security Requirements in Requirements Phase
screens.narratorSegment: Security requirements are non‑functional requirements that describe how a system protects data, maintains integrity, and resists attacks. Writing them early forces decisions: what data is sensitive, what regulatory controls apply, and which protections will be enforced. A strong security requirement is specific and testable. For instance, instead of saying 'the system must protect passwords', write 'the system must store user credentials using industry‑standard salted hashing, require a minimum password length of twelve characters, and enforce account lockout after a configurable number of failed attempts.' That level of detail guides architecture, testing, and deployment. Another common element is abuse cases: describe how a malicious actor might try to misuse a feature and derive requirements to prevent that misuse. A misconception is that security requirements slow delivery; in fact, clear requirements reduce rework. Practical tasks include identifying data sensitivity labels, listing compliance constraints, and turning each into a short requirement with an acceptance test. Try converting one feature you know into two precise security requirements and their acceptance criteria. Security Requirements in Requirements Phase means make security requirements specific and testable—define controls, metrics, and acceptance criteria up front.. In practical terms, translating risk and compliance into concrete, testable requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Security Requirements
Writing testable security requirements
Translate risk and compliance into precise acceptance criteria.
Identify assets: user credentials, personal photos, database records.
Classify sensitivity: public, internal, confidential and map protections.
Derive requirements: hashing, encryption at rest, access controls, logging, retention.
Concrete example
<Security Requirement: Login Credentials>
- Passwords MUST be stored using salted hashing with an algorithm approved by policy.
- Minimum password length: 12 characters.
- Account lockout after 5 failed attempts, reset via verified email.
- Acceptance: automated test shows stored value is not raw password and login resets correctly.
Key Takeaway

Well‑formed security requirements reduce ambiguity, guide design, and create clear tests.

screens.title: Threat Modeling and Secure Design
screens.narratorSegment: Threat modeling is a structured activity in the design phase that identifies potential threats, entry points, and mitigations. Common approaches include STRIDE—covering Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege—and complementary scoring models such as DREAD. The goal is not perfect prediction but informed choices: identify likely threats against assets and design mitigations like least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns. As an example, a web application that accepts photo uploads has assets: user credentials, photos, database, and cloud storage. Entry points include the login form and the upload A P I. Applying STRIDE, you might mark S Q L injection as a tampering risk against the database and XSS as an information disclosure risk for browsers. Mitigations would include parameterized queries and output encoding, respectively. A common misconception is that threat modeling is purely academic; instead, it produces concrete mitigations that guide implementation and testing. Your design task: pick one entry point and name two STRIDE threats and two mitigations you would include in the design review. Threat Modeling and Secure Design means use stride to map threats to assets and produce design decisions that materially reduce risk before code is written.. In practical terms, using stride and secure design principles to reduce attack surface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Threat Modeling & Design
STRIDE applied to a feature
Identify assets, entry points, STRIDE threats, and mitigations to shape design choices.
Assets
User credentials, photos, database, cloud storage
Entry Points
Login form, upload API, viewing endpoint
Example Threats
SQL injection (tampering), XSS (information disclosure)
Mitigations
  • Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection.
  • Apply output encoding and input validation to mitigate XSS.
  • Enforce least privilege for storage access and separate upload processing.
Design Principles
Apply least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns to make attacks harder and failures safer.

screens.title: Secure Coding & Early Testing Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Secure coding and early testing are the development team's daily defenses. Secure coding means choosing safe libraries, following standards that avoid common mistakes like buffer overflows or unsafe deserialization, and keeping dependencies up to date. Code review, both manual peer review and automated checks, serves as a human and machine filter. Static application security testing runs during development to detect patterns such as insecure string concatenation that could lead to S Q L injection. Dynamic tests are used later, but SAST during development finds many preventable issues early. A concrete example: flagging unsanitized input used in database calls allows a developer to switch to parameterized queries before deployment. A common misconception is that automated tools replace human judgment; they do not. Tools find patterns, humans assess context and decide whether a change is feasible and correct. Practical next steps include adding SAST to the CI pipeline, requiring a short security checklist in pull requests, and scheduling periodic dependency scans. What small CI step could you add this week to reduce risk on your team? In practical terms, how secure coding, code review, and early sast reduce defects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Development Best Practice
keyIdea.text: Combine secure coding, dependency hygiene, code review, and SAST in CI to detect and prevent defects early.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Secure Coding & Testing
Secure coding practices
Preferred habits: safe libraries, input validation, dependency management, and peer review.
  • Use well‑maintained libraries and enforce dependency scanning.
  • Perform peer code reviews that include security checklist items.
  • Automate SAST in CI to catch common patterns before merge.
  • Follow coding standards that avoid unsafe constructs and race conditions.
Code example (illustrative)
<!-- PSEUDO: avoid building queries with string concatenation -->
// Bad practice:
query = "SELECT * FROM photos WHERE owner = '" + userInput + "'";
// Good practice:
query = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM photos WHERE owner = ?");
query.bind(userInput);
results = query.execute();
Key Takeaway

Automate SAST in CI and require security items in PR reviews so risky patterns are corrected before release.

screens.title: Securing the Deployment Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is where code becomes a running service, and it is one of the most sensitive moments for security. A secure deployment includes hardening hosts, validating configuration, and ensuring that access controls and secrets are managed correctly. Hardening means reducing the attack surface: remove unused services, patch operating systems and middleware, and enforce least privilege for service accounts. Configuration validation checks that TLS is enabled, unnecessary ports are closed, and logs are captured for auditing. Access control covers both human and machine identities — provision only the permissions needed for each role and use ephemeral credentials or managed identity services when possible. Before production release, run final security checks: configuration scanning, secrets scanning, a smoke security test suite, and a short focused penetration check on exposed endpoints. A common and costly omission is assuming the deployment pipeline is safe by default; the pipeline itself needs security controls, secrets handling, and role separation so build artifacts cannot be tampered with. Example: when deploying a web app, ensure that the storage account for user photos denies public listing, the web server uses parameterized queries to talk to the database, and the firewall restricts administrative access. Misconception to avoid: deployment security is not only the ops team’s job — developers, architects, and security engineers must coordinate to ensure controls are implemented and verified. Takeaway: protect the runtime environment, validate settings programmatically, and treat deployment as another security gate that must be tested.

keyIdea.title: Deployment hardening matters
keyIdea.text: Securing servers, pipelines, and access controls before production reduces attack surface and prevents many post-deployment incidents.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.1 › Securing the Deployment Environment
Deployment

Runtime hardening and final checks

Before traffic reaches production, verify infrastructure, pipeline security, and access controls. Treat deployment as an essential security gate.

Hardening
Remove unnecessary services, apply patches, verify TLS and secure defaults.
Access Controls
Enforce least privilege for humans and service identities, use ephemeral credentials.
Pipeline security
Protect build artifacts and secrets in CI/CD. Validate artifact integrity before release.
Key Takeaway

Treat deployment as a gated security step: harden hosts, secure pipelines, and verify access policies before release.

Example Scenario

Photo app: deployment checklist

  • Ensure storage container denies public listing and uses signed URLs for access.
  • Harden web server images and remove admin ports from public subnets.
  • Rotate and store credentials in a managed secrets store, not in code or plain text.
  • Run a focused penetration check and a configuration scanner in the pipeline stage.
Deployment verification snippet (example check)
# verify TLS
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i "Strict-Transport-Security"

# check storage public access
az storage container show --name photos --query "properties.publicAccess"
Common mistake

Assuming that production settings are identical to development defaults. This mismatch often exposes services with weak configs.

screens.title: Continuous Monitoring and Vulnerability Management
screens.narratorSegment: Security does not end at deployment. Maintenance and monitoring are continuous activities that detect new threats, apply fixes, and preserve resilience. Monitoring captures logs, metrics, and alerts that help detect suspicious behavior such as repeated failed logins or unusual upload patterns. Vulnerability management means tracking findings from static and dynamic scans, penetration tests, or vendor advisories, then prioritizing and remediating them on an ongoing schedule. Regular patching, dependency updates, and library reviews reduce the window of exposure for known issues. Incident response processes should be rehearsed so teams can act quickly when monitoring surfaces a real incident. Importantly, maintenance includes validating that security controls stay effective as the application evolves — configuration drift, new integrations, or changed permissions can degrade protections. A practical example: automate periodic scans of the photo storage service to confirm ACLs and run dependency scans on server images used by your pipeline. Misconception to avoid: maintenance is not purely operational housekeeping; it should feed insights back into requirements, design, and developer training so the SSDLC improves with each cycle. Final reflective question: how will you ensure that monitoring data turns into prioritized actions, not ignored noise?

Incident response processes should be rehearsed so teams can act quickly when monitoring surfaces a real incident. Importantly, maintenance includes validating that security controls stay effective as the application evolves — configuration drift, new integrations, or changed permissions can degrade protections. A practical example: automate periodic scans of the photo storage service to confirm ACLs and run dependency scans on server images used by your pipeline. Misconception to avoid: maintenance is not purely operational housekeeping; it should feed insights back into requirements, design, and developer training so the SSDLC improves with each cycle. Final reflective question: how will you ensure that monitoring data turns into prioritized actions, not ignored noise?

Module 09 › Chapter 9.1 › Continuous Monitoring
Maintenance

Continuous monitoring and vulnerability lifecycle

Collect telemetry, triage findings, and apply fixes regularly. Make maintenance part of delivery culture.

  1. 1. Capture logs and alerts for authentication, uploads, and admin actions.
  2. 2. Triage scan and pen test results into prioritized tickets.
  3. 3. Patch dependencies and rotate secrets on schedule.
  4. 4. Run post-incident reviews and feed lessons back into design and requirements.
Monitoring
Alerts, dashboards, anomaly detection.
Vulnerability Mgmt
Prioritize and remediate based on risk and exposure.
Example

Patch workflow for a critical library

When an open-source library is disclosed as vulnerable, the team should identify impacted services, open a remediation ticket, schedule a controlled update in staging, run automated tests and security scans, and deploy the patch with deployment validation checks.

Why this works

It reduces exposure window and ensures updates do not introduce regressions while maintaining secure posture.

Key Takeaway

Monitoring and a practiced remediation process keep security active, not passive.

screens.title: Pitfalls When Implementing an SSDLC
screens.narratorSegment: Many organizations attempt to bolt security on at the end or treat the SSDLC as a one-time project. This approach creates recurring gaps and increases fix costs. Common mistakes include: treating the SSDLC as a checklist rather than a continuous program, involving security only at testing, and failing to provide developers with secure coding training. Another critical mistake is assuming that implementing a set of controls equals being secure; improper implementation can produce a false sense of safety. For example, if a team enables static scanning but ignores high-risk findings because of short deadlines, the scanning process becomes theater rather than protection. A healthier alternative is to set measurable milestones: integrate security requirements into planning, conduct threat modeling early, require code review and automated checks, and make remediation part of sprint acceptance criteria. Also ensure security professionals participate in design decisions and help prioritize mitigations based on business risk. Misconception check: security tools alone do not fix architectural weaknesses — process and culture must support the tools. Closing question: which of your current processes could unintentionally create blind spots if left unchecked?

Avoid

What not to do

Sustainable practices

Reflection

Which practice will have the most immediate impact in your team: training, earlier reviews, or automating checks in the pipeline?

screens.title: STRIDE Threat Modeling Exercise — Photo Sharing App
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical STRIDE threat model for the photo-sharing scenario. Start by listing assets: user credentials, user photos, user metadata, the application database, the web server, and cloud storage. Then identify entry points such as the login form, register form, photo upload A P I, and photo viewing endpoint. For each component, ask the STRIDE questions: can someone spoof an identity, tamper with data, deny actions, disclose information, cause denial of service, or gain elevated privileges? For example, for user authentication, spoofing is possible if credentials are weak or stolen; mitigations include strong password policies, salted hashing for stored credentials, and multi-factor authentication. For photo upload, tampering and information disclosure are risks if uploads are not validated and storage permissions are too permissive; mitigate with file type checks, virus scanning, strict ACLs, and signed access URLs. Record each threat and propose a mitigation at a high level. A common misconception is that listing a mitigation is enough—each mitigation should be actionable and assigned to an owner. Try filling the template during design reviews, and use the results to update requirements and test cases. End with the question: which threat would you prioritize first, and why?

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.1 › STRIDE Exercise
Activity template

Threat model steps

  1. Identify assets and critical data flows.
  2. Map entry points and trust boundaries.
  3. Apply STRIDE to each component or flow.
  4. Document threats and propose mitigations with owners.
  5. Feed results into requirements, design, and tests.
Filled sample: Authentication & Upload (excerpt)
# Assets:
- User credentials (hashed)
- User photos
- Database
- Web server
- Cloud storage

# Entry points:
- Login form
- Photo upload API

# Authentication (STRIDE):
Spoofing: stolen credentials -> mitigation: strong passwords, hashing, MFA
Tampering: session fixation -> mitigation: secure cookie flags, rotate tokens
Information Disclosure: credential leaks -> mitigation: hashed passwords, limit logging

# Photo upload (STRIDE):
Tampering: malicious file content -> mitigation: content-type validation, AV scanning
Information Disclosure: public storage ACLs -> mitigation: private storage + signed URLs
Denial of Service: large uploads -> mitigation: size limits, rate limiting
Example mitigations
  • Strong passwords & MFA: reduce spoofing and credential replay risk.
  • Parameterize queries: prevent SQL injection tampering against the database.
  • Signed URLs: control access to stored photos and reduce leakage.
  • Rate limits and quotas: protect endpoints from denial of service caused by abuse.
Pro tip

Use the threat model to create concrete acceptance tests. Each mitigation should map to a test or verification step.

Check your understanding

Which STRIDE category would you prioritize for the login endpoint, and what single control would reduce that risk most?

screens.title: Feedback Loops: Using Testing and Incidents to Improve the SSDLC
screens.narratorSegment: An effective SSDLC learns from tests and incidents. Results from SAST, DAST, IAST, and penetration tests should be triaged into actionable items: add or refine security requirements, adjust design decisions, or update coding standards. Incident post-mortems are equally valuable; they reveal gaps between expected and real behavior. The feedback loop should be formalized: assign remediation owners, set timelines, and verify fixes with follow-up testing. Training and documentation should also be updated when patterns of developer errors appear. For example, if multiple findings show improper input validation across services, update the requirements to mandate centralized validation libraries and add unit tests that exercise boundary cases. Avoid the misconception that remediation ends when a ticket is closed; include a verification step and a short monitoring window to confirm the fix holds in production. Use lightweight reviews and periodic audits to ensure the SSDLC itself evolves as the software and threat landscape change. Final learner check: after a penetration test uncovers a design-level flaw, which part of the SSDLC should change first — requirements, design, or testing — and why? Feedback Loops: Using Testing and Incidents to Improve the SSDLC means feed testing and incident insights back into requirements, design, and training to continuously strengthen security.. In practical terms, turn findings into better requirements, design, and developer practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three essential concepts to keep at the front of your mind when working with secure development. First, the Secure Software Development Life Cycle is the practice of integrating security activities into every phase of development so risks are found and mitigated earlier. Second, the "shift left" principle means moving security tasks toward requirements and design; doing this reduces the cost and effort of fixes later in the cycle. Third, threat modeling is a structured way to identify likely threats and their impact; methodologies like STRIDE help teams categorize risks and choose mitigations. Each of these ideas supports the same goal: early, repeatable, and practical security decisions that scale with software. As you move between planning, building, and operating systems, let these concepts guide choices that minimize surprises and create measurable improvements over time.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: Three more compact concepts reinforce secure design and planning. Security requirements are non-functional needs that specify how data must be protected and what controls must be present; they translate business and regulatory constraints into testable criteria. fullNarratorScript:
We begin by framing why security must be part of every step of delivery, not an afterthought. The Secure Software Development Life Cycle or SSDLC extends the traditional SDLC by weaving security activities into requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. That shift prevents costly rework, reduces exploit windows, and creates measurable controls. For example, defining security requirements with functional requirements means authentication, data classification, and storage protections are considered before design decisions lock them out. A well‑run SSDLC applies threat modeling during design to uncover issues like S Q L injection or cross‑site scripting before code is written. It uses secure coding practices and code reviews during development, automated and manual testing during test cycles, and environment hardening for deployment. Finally, maintenance keeps the system resilient through monitoring and timely patches. A common mistake is treating SSDLC as a checkbox project; instead, treat it as continuous engineering. As you study this chapter, think about one system you know and how a single security requirement could have avoided a later incident.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the foundational principles and phases of an integrated Secure Software Development Life Cycle, describe the shift left security paradigm and its practical benefits, and identify where security activities belong in each SDLC phase. You will also be able to perform a basic threat modeling exercise using STRIDE to pinpoint likely weaknesses in a design and formulate clear security requirements to include in project planning. These outcomes matter because they turn security from a gate at the end of delivery into engineering choices that save time and prevent breaches. For example, defining credential handling rules in requirements reduces the chance that a later design will rely on weak storage or naive authentication. Over the next screens you will practice mapping threats to mitigations and writing one or two security requirements for a sample feature. That practical work will make the SSDLC concrete and repeatable in your team.

These practical outcomes focus on habits you can use immediately. You will practice writing security requirements that pair with functional requests, for example specifying password hashing algorithms and rotation policy alongside a login feature. You will conduct a structured threat modeling exercise on a simple web feature using STRIDE to identify spoofing, tampering, information disclosure and other threats, and then propose mitigations. You will learn to choose the right testing approaches such as static analysis during development and dynamic testing before release. Finally, you will learn maintenance practices like vulnerability management and monitoring so that your security posture adapts over time. Each objective includes an applied milestone, so you can measure progress: a written requirement, a short threat model, an SAST report review, and a deployment hardening checklist. These tasks convert concept into repeatable engineering steps that reduce surprises late in delivery.

The Secure Software Development Life Cycle is an extension of the traditional SDLC that embeds security activities and thinking into every phase of delivery. Define the SSDLC as the union of development stages plus explicit security tasks for requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Practically, that starts by making security requirements part of the project scope: classify sensitive data, require strong credential handling, and capture compliance needs. During design, do threat modeling to find attack routes and document mitigations. During development, require secure libraries, coding standards, and code reviews. During testing, run static and dynamic tools and validate mitigations with penetration tests. For deployment, harden runtime and configuration. For maintenance, monitor, patch, and manage vulnerabilities. A concrete example: a login feature should have a security requirement to store passwords with industry‑standard hashing and to rate limit failed attempts. A common misconception is that SSDLC is an add‑on phase at the end of the project; instead, it is a continuous set of activities that move left. Key takeaway: when security is planned, it becomes an engineering decision rather than a last‑minute rescue. How would you capture one security requirement for a simple feature you maintain?

Shift left is a change in mindset: insert security activities earlier in development so defects are found when they cost less to fix. The principle arises from the observation that the cost and effort to remediate vulnerabilities increase sharply the later they are discovered. When a design flaw is corrected at the requirements phase, it may require a single decision; when the same flaw is fixed in production, it may require code changes, retesting, redeployment, and potential incident response. To adopt shift left you change workflows: require security requirements during planning, run threat models during design, and enforce static analysis and code reviews during development. A practical example: adding a requirement to salt and hash passwords removes the need for later emergency rework to replace insecure storage. Common misconceptions include thinking shift left eliminates the need for testing; it does not. Rather, it changes the types of testing earlier and reduces the number of critical issues found late. Key exercises include capturing one security requirement per feature and requiring a short design review that includes a threat model. How would you redesign a planning checklist to ensure a security requirement cannot be skipped?

Security requirements are non‑functional requirements that describe how a system protects data, maintains integrity, and resists attacks. Writing them early forces decisions: what data is sensitive, what regulatory controls apply, and which protections will be enforced. A strong security requirement is specific and testable. For instance, instead of saying 'the system must protect passwords', write 'the system must store user credentials using industry‑standard salted hashing, require a minimum password length of twelve characters, and enforce account lockout after a configurable number of failed attempts.' That level of detail guides architecture, testing, and deployment. Another common element is abuse cases: describe how a malicious actor might try to misuse a feature and derive requirements to prevent that misuse. A misconception is that security requirements slow delivery; in fact, clear requirements reduce rework. Practical tasks include identifying data sensitivity labels, listing compliance constraints, and turning each into a short requirement with an acceptance test. Try converting one feature you know into two precise security requirements and their acceptance criteria. Security Requirements in Requirements Phase means make security requirements specific and testable—define controls, metrics, and acceptance criteria up front.. In practical terms, translating risk and compliance into concrete, testable requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Threat modeling is a structured activity in the design phase that identifies potential threats, entry points, and mitigations. Common approaches include STRIDE—covering Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege—and complementary scoring models such as DREAD. The goal is not perfect prediction but informed choices: identify likely threats against assets and design mitigations like least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns. As an example, a web application that accepts photo uploads has assets: user credentials, photos, database, and cloud storage. Entry points include the login form and the upload A P I. Applying STRIDE, you might mark S Q L injection as a tampering risk against the database and XSS as an information disclosure risk for browsers. Mitigations would include parameterized queries and output encoding, respectively. A common misconception is that threat modeling is purely academic; instead, it produces concrete mitigations that guide implementation and testing. Your design task: pick one entry point and name two STRIDE threats and two mitigations you would include in the design review. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Secure coding and early testing are the development team's daily defenses. Secure coding means choosing safe libraries, following standards that avoid common mistakes like buffer overflows or unsafe deserialization, and keeping dependencies up to date. Code review, both manual peer review and automated checks, serves as a human and machine filter. Static application security testing runs during development to detect patterns such as insecure string concatenation that could lead to S Q L injection. Dynamic tests are used later, but SAST during development finds many preventable issues early. A concrete example: flagging unsanitized input used in database calls allows a developer to switch to parameterized queries before deployment. Deployment is where code becomes a running service, and it is one of the most sensitive moments for security. Here are three essential concepts to keep at the front of your mind when working with secure development. First, the Secure Software Development Life Cycle is the practice of integrating security activities into every phase of development so risks are found and mitigated earlier. Second, the "shift left" principle means moving security tasks toward requirements and design; doing this reduces the cost and effort of fixes later in the cycle. Third, threat modeling is a structured way to identify likely threats and their impact; methodologies like STRIDE help teams categorize risks and choose mitigations. Each of these ideas supports the same goal: early, repeatable, and practical security decisions that scale with software. As you move between planning, building, and operating systems, let these concepts guide choices that minimize surprises and create measurable improvements over time.

Three more compact concepts reinforce secure design and planning. Security requirements are non-functional needs that specify how data must be protected and what controls must be present; they translate business and regulatory constraints into testable criteria. Secure design principles such as least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns guide architecture decisions to limit the blast radius of failures. An abuse case is a scenario describing how an attacker might misuse a system; using abuse cases helps teams discover realistic threats and write requirements and tests that address real misuse patterns. Together these concepts help teams design systems that are resilient, testable, and aligned with business risk rather than dependent on informal assumptions.
